--- 帖子 #41233 ---
For me, i allocate 1-1.5% per pair, dividing the position to 5 small trades (if 1 percent) and 6-7 small trades (if 1.5%). Each position has a 100 pip SL. If they get taken out, they get taken out, but i rarely allow that to happen. Before placing a trade i determine the size beforehand (1% risk, 100 pip SL) and just divide accordingly. Take profit is based on market structure (on 30 min) looking left and whether or not price is at a major area of support and resistance on the daily (then i target farther market structures). how do u guys do it, suggestions are welcome too

We cant know obviously how market will act before hand but we are already prepared to act accordingly.Its important if you do sell prior of event and price does drop 6850-45 you should get out and anticipate another push up to 6880 or even 69.Point here dont get stuck selling before the event.I want you guys develop conscious awareness of event and market moves prior and after event. Remember when trading USD its important to understand its strengths can overtake other currencies fundamentals hence despite everything I wrote price can smash down 68.20-68 before the event. When I am not sure direction of USD I consciously shift my focus on none USD pairs like AUD ,CAD crosses which are my favorites. AUD/NZD falls in this category. That possibility is there!In short trading is fluid activity its constantly shifting and you got to get in sink with the market.Get in the zone! Here is to next week

Hi guys There is a lot of talk about position size. My view is if you can make more money working at minimum job then trading then you are doing disservice to yourself.Let me explain suppose you open typical 500 dollar account and trade 10c size you could make money however amount of effort vs time invested becomes worthless furthermore because gains and losses are so minuscule you are not getting psychological impact that requires in real trading.Often you hear people say no more then 1% account on any position.To me this is wrong position size is depended on skill level.I often risk over 10% and rip the rewards.I have specific goal I want to achieve and 1% is not gonna do it. In short risk what you are comfortable with and have exit strategy to get out if it does not work out.

Little trading lesson When you see chart like this AC its tempting to short.While you might get lucky few times but do it 10x I bet you will lose big time. People posting high win ratios are meaningless stats.Means very little. Care about DD and account preservation.

I find trading inspiration in the arts as weird as that sounds.Remarkable artists overcoming adversary inspires me and you should be as well I love Pat Martino RIP saw him in jazz club in Cambridge.After concert I gifted him my artwork and he graciously accepted and invited me to his house in Philadelphia.Didn't get to see him again then he passed away. He is special remarkable talent.He had a brain injury and lost all his ability to play guitar and had to re learn everything again! His albums after recovery are remarkable as well. That evolution was suddenly interrupted in 1980 when Martino suffered the near-fatal seizure that left him to rebuild his memory and his career from scratch. He had been born with an arteriovenous malformation, a condition that had led him to suffer hallucinations and seizures since childhood but remained misdiagnosed. Martino emerged from the experience with a newfound, Zen-like outlook. In an interview for the Philadelphia Inquirer in 2011, he referred to the experience as "the greatest thing that ever happened to me." While his philosophical bent was presaged by titles like "Consciousness" and "Where Love's a Grown-Up God," the guitarist later viewed the early part of his career as driven more by ambition than art. "My career literally came to an end at that very moment," he said of the surgery. "From that point forward, my interest was no longer in my profession; my interest was in survival as a human being. It erased the blackboard, and I found myself in the same position as I was as a child." Following his surgery in 1980, Martino spent several years relearning the instrument, listening back to his own recordings and struggling with depression and the grueling process of recovering his skills. He reemerged in 1987 with The Return , which showcased a miraculous virtuosity seemingly undiminished by his brush with death and amnesia. https://www.npr.org/2021/11/02/10514...ver-dies-at-77 Inserted Video Inserted Video

--- 帖子 #41489 ---
Hi Dirlik, No problem with the delay. I personally do not use arrows, some people find them helpful. I have seen them used in systems with success. The pivots 'method' is based on various MT4 indicators listed on the first post. I use Davit's template with its indicators. Paired with the markets fundamental behavior, you can define entry and exit points you are comfortable with. For me, that means generally R61 to the WPP, or S61 to the WPP. The further a pair pulls away from the WPP, the higher the chances it will be 'pulled' back to the WPP. Fundamentals can drive a pair up to the 78 and 100 levels and beyond, I have noticed though that once it passes 138, it is reversing and is less likely to return to WPP. It also means getting to know certain pairs. You can see what Davit recommends. It helps to read and reread the first post, then start moving through the thread. I also keep up with the thread moving forward. You can see Davits current thoughts. And learn how to develop your own, as it relates to this system. I have traded for years, but it wasn't until I started with this system that I actually got out of the 'red'. Take your time and learn, if you want to become the best trader you can be. As Davit mentions, it is simple but advanced. There is no EA, it is manual judgement.

--- 帖子 #41527 ---
Important for today, big news tonight. Read it somewhere online. Hope would be helpful. What is expected from the BoJ? Last week we saw an article in the Japanese publication Yomiuri Shimbun that the BoJ was reviewing the negative effects of its current monetary policy regime – despite only changing its policy setting on 20 December, where they lifted the ceiling (or cap) by which the 10yr JGB yield (Japanese govt bond) can trade to 0.50%, the market swiftly took this to mean another key change was incoming. The fact the BoJ had to ramp up its daily bond buying to a record amount to defend the 0.50% cap, suggests their policy setting is still highly dysfunctional, and with inflation pushing 4% its current yield curve control (YCC) program is on borrowed time. While we can look at the possible outcomes, and assign a probability and potential market reaction, I think in all cases the BoJ will try its utmost to say the action is designed to address an increasingly dysfunctional market and should not be seen as a tightening of policy. The market will likely look through this and ignore their pleas. Given 10yr JGBs currently trade above 0.5% (or 50bp), 10yr swap rates trade above 90bp and the JPY has had a one-way move of late, one assumes the market is skewed and part positioned to an outcome that the BoJ abolish its YCC program. This plays into my back-of-the-envelope playbook. Possible actions: • The BoJ again widens the yield band to -/+0.75% while continuing to buy incredible amounts of JGBs in its daily operations to support the 0.75% yield cap - an action that doesn’t make a huge amount of sense as it would not resolve the dysfunctional market and would need to be altered again – likely promotes a 2%+ rally on the day in USDJPY • The BoJ widens the yield band out to -/+1% while continuing to buy JGBs to support the cap – tactically this makes more sense, but an action that could cause a 1%+ rally in USDJPY • The BoJ leave policy unchanged but signals a change is coming – this would surprise and cause a 2.5%+ rally on the day in USDJPY • Completely terminates its YCC program – the market is leaning this way but would still likely cause a 3%+ sell-off on the day in USDJPY • Shifts the YCC target which is currently capping 10yr JGBs at 0.50% and move to target the 5yr JGB instead – it's hard to create a clear framework on this policy change, but an action that likely leads to the most subdued reaction seen in USDJPY

Industry always markets that you must have hard stops.That's because brokers make their money on them!Why they use in house algos to trigger the spikes at closings or openings! Its fine! Dont beat yourself.Always always forgive yourself! allow yourself to improve This is from PDF on clipboard under Davit's Philosophy.Obviously changed the title for copy rights reasons Chapter 24 FORGIVENESS One of the biggest problems I see with traders is that they refuse to forgive themselves for trading mistakes. This causes a much bigger problem than most people realize. You see, when you make a trading mistake, you need to forgive yourself for making that mistake. But the thing is many people do not forgive themselves for their mistakes. In fact, they do quite the opposite. They beat themselves up and continually picture what they did wrong in vivid detail. This is the very worst thing you can do after making a mistake, trading or otherwise. Forgiveness is a key concept in Psycho-Cybernetics. As weve just learned about how our subconscious works, we know that if we continually picture in vivid detail something, it causes that picture to come true for us. Or it at least makes it much more likely for it to come true. So it only makes sense that if we make a mistake, we must forget that mistake and forgive ourselves completely. If, on the other hand, we dont forgive ourselves and relive the mistake in our minds again and again, what do you think is going to happen? Its obvious that we will repeat the mistake. This happens because our subconscious does not care whether we give it good or bad information, it simply sees the clear pictures we give it and tries to act it out in our lives. Obviously, it can only act this picture out if its within our capabilities. And I think we all know that making trading mistakes is quite within our capabilities. This is the reason it is so important to forgive ourselves when we make a mistake or an error. If we dont, we are likely to relive the mistake in our minds and then most likely project it onto our trading. This will cause big problems. If you think back, Im sure can you think of times where you made mistakes and beat yourself up for it. Not forgiving yourself, no matter what the mistake, will bring out the worst emotions. Remorse, regret, self-doubt, and guilt all come with not forgiving ourselves for a past mistake. Youve heard it all before. Im sure youve been told to forget a past losing trade and move on to the next one. Emotions are used correctly and appropriately when it applies to something in the present time. Since we cannot live in the past, we cant appropriately react emotionally to the past. As Dr. Maltz says, The past can be simply written off, closed, forgotten, insofar as our emotional reactions are concerned. We do not need to take an emotional position one way or the other regarding detours that might have taken us off course in the past. The important thing is our present direction and our present goal. We need to recognize our own errors as mistakes. Otherwise, we could not correct our course and steering or guidance would be impossible. But it is futile and fatal to hate or condemn ourselves for our mistakes. One of the biggest reasons people get into losing streaks while trading is because they confuse their losing trades with themselves. In other words, we conclude that because we had a losing trade or a series of losing trades, we are a losing trader. But the important thing to remember here is we are not our losing trades. Losing trades are part of trading. There isnt a single trader in the world who doesnt have losing trades. The only way to avoid them is not to trade in the first place. You cannot be a successful trader until you take mistakes and losing trades for what they really are. They are simply by-products in the trading game and need to be used to gain learning and understanding. But in no way do they define us as a person. But that is where the big problem comes in. Many people let their losing trades and mistakes define them. If they're having trouble and have had a series of losing trades, they start to think of themselves as a loser. They continually think of themselves in that way. As we know from before, this kind of thinking will just bring on more of the same. Forgiving yourself completely is the only way to avoid this trouble. You are not your mistakes and losing trades. You must put the past behind you and go forward. Holding a grudge against yourself only hurts yourself. Forgive yourself, its the only way to be successful. Above its extremely important paradigm shift how you see trading and how you see mistakes and losers.To me its where one should be ideally or strive to reach.Once you truly grasp probability factor of my system then a loser is just a statistic by product of sample..Its all probability over series of trades and like MD says on my 1st page "You don’t need to know what is going to happen next in order to make money." Its so simple and profound same time.I still get chills reading simple things like this by Mark Douglas

The samples for the Surveys of Consumers are statistically designed to be representative of all American households, excluding those in Alaska and Hawaii. --- 帖子 #42117 ---
Every weekend, in addition to the calendar, I find it very helpful to pull up weekly and daily charts (on another platform, without pivots) and just draw horizontal lines at support and resistance on the higher TFs. You will be amazed at what jumps out at you, especially where you see spike highs and lows with pinbars. When these areas line up with a weekly pivot and/or ADR, I won't say "risk free" trade, but the higher the TF the stronger the support and resistance. It is just basic supply and demand economics. No lagging indicators required!

--- 帖子 #42119 ---

--- 帖子 #42120 ---
Definitely a good idea, there's a book that goes into this stuff. Naked charts + Sup/Res on higher time frames and candlestick patterns for reversals. Mixed this with Davits Pivots and never looked back. Attached the book for anyone that wants it. He renames a lot of the stuff, e.g. Pinbars = Kangaroo tails, Double tops = Moolahs etc but the principles the same

--- 帖子 #42261 ---
Hi All, I just wanted to share something that may seem obvious but can take years to understand. There is enough. There are enough pips in this market for everyone. If you study the thread, and learn from Davit and others, you will be able to succeed as a trader. Success is a relative term, you have to know what that means for you. Here are some sentiments I have seen in myself. "Geez, I got out way to soon!" There is enough though and you will have another opportunity. "Dang, the trade has turned against me! I entered at a good pivot point!" Ask yourself, do the fundamentals agree with my original entry(or ME's). And what is the PA doing? Decide whether it makes sense to stay in the trade or exit. And remember... There is enough. If I have to exit and take a loss, I can take another trade. Losses happen. Keep studying the nuggets here. Such as the one above from Davit "if you are nervous about your trade, you lot size may be too big". At every moment, the market is changing. Having a edge, like this system, will give you success over time. The biggest challenge for me has been mastering myself and remembering, THERE IS ENOUGH FOR ALL OF US. Enough philosophy, lets trade!

Analysis This trade was opened on a Friday towards evening, I try not to trade on Fridays and certainly not to open trades towards evening, well...you can see the result. 1 - Interesting level of R + WR38 2 - TDI at good levels (1H + 4H TF ) 3 - ADR hasn't crossed 100% yet (I think it was 95%?) Good combina tion, why not wait a while and enter the trade, I like to have a closed week though, I don't like to carry trades over to the next week, there would have to be a reason atp, but generally for me week = all closed, anyway everyone's business. I entered the trade with a bit more position, not that it would have derailed me in any way, the account could handle a lot more. But something didn't sit right with me then ( generally speaking, screw hunches, be like a robot = take over yourself), I just entered on a Friday and it annoyed me. I had tw o options, maybe still load up and spin, or close with a small loss and move on. I closed in the morning and it was a mistake, I couldn't get to the PC and had to leave, so the check was only done on mobile. The upshot of this is that I protected capital rather than risk a big move against me and take a bigger loss which would then take longer to replace. Better to close out, make money with the next trade. With a trade I say to myself = am I protecting my capital enough? Have I done the best I can for it? Everyone knows full well that keeping an open position is harder than closing a losing position thinking that now it will turn around... With that mindset, you are at the mercy of the market, you lose the ability to make decisions, and when you fall on a margin call, you no longer make decisions Attached Image (click to enlarge) My point was, don't take a bad trade, accept it, take the loss, do the analysis of why it came to this, learn your lesson and move on.. yeah and take a look at the balance and say to yourself...yeah I can move on at all.

--- 帖子 #42288 ---
Had this exact same conversation in my head with this EG trade. 4 positions opened initially, however, they were prematurely opened (in hindsight). After closing 3 in loss, I noticed price forming long wicked bullish candles. I then decided to open 1 more and keep the latest position open, and targeted the last "unfilled" wick to the left. Closed for some profit, reducing the overall loss. Takeaways: Don’t open positions directly after a large candle closes. Wait for signs of price slowing down (braking) and for PA to form candlestick patterns toward your bias. Another more "suitable" zone was present on S78. I was indecisive throughout the entire trade, and struggled to find objective reasons to stay in the trade. When in doubt, stay out or in this case, get out.

Great Chess Quotes For Traders: Great chess quotes from Garry Kasparov that can apply to chess, trading, and daily life. 1. You must know what questions to ask and ask them frequently. Questions are what matters. Questions, and discovering the right ones, are the key to staying on course. 2. The top achievers believe in themselves and their plans, and they work constantly to ensure those plans are worthy of their belief. 3. Personal style is not generic software that you can download. You must instead recognize what works best for you and then, through trial and error, develop your own method- your own map. 4. We must also avoid being distracted from our strategic path by the competition. 5. Play the opening like a book, the middle game like a magician, and the endgame like a machine. 6. You may learn much more from a game you lose than from a game you win. You will have to lose hundreds of games before becoming a good player. 7. Chess is everything: art, science, and sport. 8. By all means examine the games of the great chess players, but don’t swallow them whole. Their games are valuable not for their separate moves, but for their vision of chess, their way of thinking. 9. Steady effort pays off, even if not always in an immediate, tangible way. 10. Everyone must create his own successful combinations with the ingredients he has. There are guidelines for what works, but each person has to discover what works for him. This doesn’t happen by itself. Through practice and observation, you must take an active role in your own education. 11. Success and satisfaction may be our goals, but they can also lead to bad habits that will impede greater success and satisfaction. 12. Choose your move carefully, in chess as in life.

--- 帖子 #43142 ---
I understand the advantage of dividing the order size into many small lots, which is something I always do. However, I don't understand the rationale behind placing many tiny orders with a distance of only 1 pip or less between them.

--- 帖子 #43143 ---
Different stops and targets. You may want a certain size position, but based on your risk, you may not wish to hold the ENTIRE position should it move against you. You can then save those that closed to reenter at a better price should it keep moving against you. On the flip side, you may wish to hold some of the position all the way to the original target, but price action may lead you to close out some prior.

--- 帖子 #43144 ---
My observation in regard to this is: It is necessary. What I observe is when you open the position the price move positive a small bit and make you happy and then suddenly it moves up against you. If the price move down when you open you will get good money but the price move against you so when it retraces you will make less money or probably break even. You will make break even as you get scared that the price move against you now it is time you exit before I go in negative again. Psychology-fear game. This is what market want. And slowly it moves against you, the more you open, the more it moves against you, but there is a saturation point. That is where you kill the market.

--- 帖子 #43145 ---
Thank you for sharing your thoughts. I agree that breaking positions into smaller parts based on risk management is an effective strategy. However, implementing it with FIFO rules can be challenging. I used to follow a similar approach, and it worked well for me, particularly during DD. I was able to make many trades with profit until I closed the original orders. However, I've become more cautious now and need to keep track of each closed order's profit and loss. With FIFO rules, I have to close the original position when I want to close other trades in profit. Although it can be tedious, it's essential to maintain discipline and manage risk effectively.

--- 帖子 #43149 ---
I used offshore brokers for 6 years from 2014-2020. The regulation is a false sense of security as funds are not protected in the US. I was able to use 5-10% of the margin trading offshore as I would have needed in the US. Not to mention, ironically, the conditions are far superior as far as spreads , commission and overall performance. In 2020, I discovered prop firms. I am funded with 4 of them. I no longer trade with brokers at all except for DOW and NAS futures at AMP. The trick with the props is you must base your risk on the "max loss" allowed, which is normally 10% of the account equity. So if you are funded 100K with 10% max loss, you are really funded 10K. So if you have DD of say 20% on max loss, it is really only 2% of the account equity. With the offshore options and the prop options, I truly cannot see why anyone would trade with these shithole offerings in the US.

--- 帖子 #43375 ---
I used hard stops on the silver trade. I haven't always traded with stops, it depends on my confidence in the trade and the risk. This went horribly wrong with EA trades as you may of seen from previous posts but holding out paid off and they came good. This has made me re-evaluate the way I trade and will certainly be trading more cautiously with more stops going forward. I use both the higher and lower TF to decide where to place stops, not too tight and not too wide to allow the trade to 'breathe'. The times price has stopped me out of a trade and then bounced up or down.. so frustrating! I try and think where I want my stop to be, where price won't go but at the same time offers a safety blanket and keeps me in the trade. Its a tough one.

Just wanted to share my recent trading journey with you all, and boy, it's been quite a ride! This month, I faced my biggest loss in the past two years, and I thought it'd be cool to remind myself (and you guys) about the mistakes I made along the way. First things first, I always check those pivot lines from last month! If I had bothered to glance at the EU and UJ lines from last month, I would've dodged these bad trades. Lesson learned. I also made the silly mistake of adding more positions way too soon. I mean, what was I thinking? That's not my style at all! It's like I temporarily forgot all my trading smarts. Now, the loss is still hanging over my account, and I'm in the red DD territory. The big question for me is whether to close or hold these positions for the upcoming week. Tough decision, but I'm on it! Listen, I hope I'm not bumming you out with these negative report. But it's trading, and we still have two more weeks to do better. Losses are part of the trading journey, and we always move on, ready for the next opportunity. My aim here is to remind us all about the importance of sticking to our own trading rules. So, guess what? I'm creating a trusty checklist of my trade rules, my trading Bible, if you will. Gonna keep it close and consult it before every trade. No more silly slip-ups! Let's learn from our blunders and keep growing as traders. Cheers to better trades and brighter days!

--- 帖子 #43446 ---
Mark Douglas discusses the concept of cutting losses earlier in his book "Trading in the Zone." Here's a breakdown of his ideas on this topic: Identifying the signs of a potential losing trade: Douglas emphasizes the importance of recognizing warning signs that indicate a trade might not be going as expected. This includes paying attention to price movements, market conditions, and any factors that may invalidate the initial trade premise. By identifying these signs early on, traders can take action to minimize potential losses. Having a predefined exit strategy: Douglas advises traders to have a clear exit strategy before entering a trade. This includes determining specific criteria or indicators that, if met, would prompt them to exit the trade. By setting predefined exit points, traders can make rational decisions based on their trading plan, rather than succumbing to emotions or clinging to hope in the face of mounting losses. Being flexible and adaptive: While it's important to have a predefined exit strategy, Douglas also emphasizes the need for flexibility and adaptability in trading. Market conditions can change rapidly, and a trader should be willing to reassess their position if new information suggests that cutting losses earlier would be more beneficial. Being open to adjusting one's trading decisions based on evolving market dynamics is essential. Avoiding the sunk cost fallacy: One common mistake traders make is holding onto losing trades for too long, hoping for a reversal that may never come. Douglas warns against falling into the sunk cost fallacy, which refers to the tendency to make decisions based on the resources already invested (time, money, effort) rather than objectively evaluating the current situation. Traders should be willing to cut their losses early and move on to other opportunities if a trade is not performing as expected. Maintaining discipline and emotional control: Cutting losses earlier requires discipline and emotional control. Traders must resist the temptation to let losses accumulate or deviate from their predefined exit strategy due to fear, greed, or other emotions. Following a well-defined trading plan and sticking to the predetermined risk parameters can help traders make objective decisions and avoid detrimental emotional biases.

--- 帖子 #43834 ---
Hello there, Davits first post is pretty good with telling you how to set up your charts. It is a good idea to start in the beginning and start reading the posts through. Over the years, Davit has revised and updated the template he uses, as have many of us. It helps to see the ebb and flow of this system and how it works in the real world. It does not work on MT5. Keep in mind that PA is king/queen. Every system is not 100% foolproof although this one does give an edge. You have to decide what your own stop loss philosophy is going to be, what money management style works for you, etc. No one has all the answers. Most people trade for years and years before they find what works for them. Even then, expect to take losses. Find a way that you can mentally be okay with that, accept your losses and move on. I personally have traded since 2008 and still take losses, if you can learn from that, find the edge that works for you and continue on, you can become a successful trader. Best of luck.

Dont get me wrong though, im pretty familiar with DCA, I was in a paid group for a while where we used it, one of the patterns though was that alot of guys would have several green days and even green weeks in a row due to the relatively easy targets along with the staged orders and room to breathe.....but there was always that time where it just wouldnt come back, and that would wipe out several days or even weeks of profit. In other words I found it noticable in the group what the impact of a loss was like when compared to the standard stop loss/risk reward profile thats more commonly used. I.E if trader takes 2-3 hits in a week with 0.5% or 1% risk, its not all that bad, and pretty much expected. But those bigger averaged in trades have a much bigger impact. --- 帖子 #43863 ---
Not necessarily increasing the lot size as this would likely be considered as martingale. But using a lot size that over 3 entries takes you to your decided loss/stop loss amount. For example, and shown in the screenshots, if I want to risk around $500 per trade, I know that if my first entry stop loss is $200, that will give me the lot size to use for the remaining two entries, which in this case for AUDCAD would be 0.16 lots, and comes to just under $500. I used 161 for the stop loss in this example and obviously in the real world the entries wouldn't be bang on the pivots due to PA. Its just an idea though, again would be interesting to hear how others do it, doing it this way though your winrate would have to be very good as wouldnt want to be getting stung with a string of 3 entry losses, but then again, if its reached your fixed dollar amount then you've got to cut it off anyway.

--- 帖子 #43894 ---
I think you will find that indi is Nostromo's code. If so it should be this...... Attached File(s) WP_Nostromo_mod.mq4 22 KB | 331 downloads These are a few of the settings that are available. The example chart shows "Count period" as 2. For backtesting, this can be increased to show as many weeks (or days months etc) as requied. For normal trading, I prefer to show only the current week(1). That will reduce the "clutter" on the chart. I have also shown "Plot future pivots" as TRUE. These will obviously change as the week progresses and mean nothing, but are valuable for doing analysis over the weekend AFTER close of business if that is of benefit. Weekly fibs are also an option. I have found that these levels can (and are) respected across a lot of pairs. I personally only use the weekly pivots and fibs, but the "Time period" setting has several options for whatever suits. There are obviously numerous other options/settings to select from, but I have shown an example of my settings as per the attached chart. There is no need for any GMT time differences as the code is looking at the last completed(closed) candle. There will obviously be slight differences in some price levels between different brokers, because of different open and close pricing, but (certainly with the weekly pivots) there should be only a minimal difference. Attached Image (click to enlarge) These are the settings for the chart above. Attached Image (click to enlarge) I hope this helps some and please ignore if it is of no use to you. Cheers Michael

--- 帖子 #44105 ---
What I find very important is lot size adjustment, this will vary depending on the currency pair or product I’m trading. If I have less confidence in the trade or if there are some unknowns or news releases for example then I may reduce my lot size to try and minimise the risk. You shouldn't expect to enter every trade with the same lot size. I do not always trade with a S/L, if I do, I will place my stop where I’m not likely to be stopped out but where I’m comfortable that if a trade goes against me I will be stopped out to reduce my losses. If I’m unsure or less confident I will trade with much tighter stops, get stopped out and then look to re-enter at a better price when more overextended. I generally find stops quite restrictive and the number of times I’ve been stopped out but only just by a few pips and then the trade moved in my favour. This is mostly down to experience. Of course, we should only really be taking very high probability trades and should look for what I call the overall ‘story’ or confluence which could be pivots level/price level, ADR reached, S/R, signals (such as pinbar), price action, news and events.. all these elements aligning at the same time for a higher probability trade. If I trade without stops, and the trade goes against me, then I would look to scale out gradually if price does not turn, but this does depend on account size as this is not always possible. It’s probably better to get stopped out and re-enter when higher probability. This is my personal approach that should not be copied as everyone is different and with a different account sizes etc. Everyone should develop and stick to their own risk management strategy that works for them individually. I hope this helps. Regards

HI TortoiseFX, I eat, sleep and breathe trading.. Every spare moment I have I will be looking at charts and looking for the next trade/ opportunity. I do have a full time job so I have to fit trading in the evenings and at any other opportunity I have. What I believe is crucially important is chart time. Getting as much chart time as possible, simply watching charts to monitor and understand price action and what influences the markets. I will typically look at the higher time frames at the ‘bigger picture’, direction or ‘overall story’ then drop down to smaller timeframes for entries /exits etc. So, in a word, yes, I’m glued to the charts every day, as soon as I wake up, during the day (when I can) and all evening. If I don't have access to my MT4 account I will monitor the charts on my phone. I look closely as news events and make sure I know when these are occurring, I watch for price action before, during and after and try to learn from and understand how/why any data / news impacts on the markets/price. For me trading is a passion and one of those things I want to succeed at. It doesn’t happen over night and takes work, dedication and lots and lots of experience. I’m always willing to learn and still have lots to learn. I will look at and review all of my trades to analyse what went wrong and how could I have done better in terms of my entry or exit. Every week I go through the calendar for the week ahead so I know what is happening and I prepare for those news events/data and then try and align them to a trade. Each weekend I go through all of my charts and do further analysis. (Technical and fundamental). I hope that helps to answer your question. Regards N

I don't particularly like the 'Davits Pivot V3.2 Auto' version, but even so, I fixed a minor bug that affected the open price when brokercandle=true (but it doesn't affect the default pivot method, (H+L+C)/3 ). I also added some comments in the indicator for how to set and verify the correct choice of brokercandle, and of the very important timeZoneOfData setting. The choice of brokercandle = "false" *might* work, BUT you must carefully verify the right choice for timeZoneOfData. The default was -5, but I found that -6 was required. In 2 posts above, the user's choice was '0', but the only way to know what's right is to check on an H1 chart where does it draw the " Start " line. When correct, the Start line will be the first bar of the week, after the weekend gap. Unfortunately, the right answer might need changing per USA DST dates, but I don't know. Just 1 post prior suggested to use 'Pivot Voty'. I actually prefer the way that it can show the correct pivot calculations for each Week (or Month or Day). However, the method it uses is exactly the same as 'brokercandle=true'. Therefore, it is the right tool and method for brokers using 'NY-7' timezone (also inaccurately called "GMT+2"). Almost all brokers that have 5 Daily-bars-per-week are this 'NY-7' timezone. (By the way, there is no way in MT4 to determine what is the actual broker timezone; one has to inspect the bars, and to observe YEAR-ROUND what hours it reports and when/if does it change DST). I am fortunate to use broker feeds that (mostly) have 5-Daily-bars-per-week, and are the preferred 'NY-7' timezone. Therefore, using 'brokercandle=true' works just fine for me, or I can use the Pivot Voty indicator as well. Same pivots. I don't endorse this indicator, but I made 1 simple bug fix and added some comments in the Input variables section to help users make the right choices.

R38 = PP + (lastweek high - lastweek low) *0,382 R61 = PP + (lastweek high - lastweek low) *0,618 etc S38 = PP - (lastweek high - lastweek low) *0,382 etc

News events give me a view , usually , of where the PROBABILITY OF A PRICE ACTION REVERSAL where occur , and , is almost always NEAR a Pivot Point. Positive News doesn't guarantee me that PRICE is going to move in a particular direction. Market structure is the key , and , it coincides with Davit's Pivot Points. Sincerely , GE
